• Homepage: https://bend-lang.com/
  • GitHub repository: https://github.com/bendlang/bend

The developers of Bend 2 claim that it outperforms every proof assistant, including Lean, by several OOMs. It seems Victor Taelin, founder of HigherOrderCO, created the Bend 2 language.

Someone told me to check this out, and I'd like to hear your opinions.

From https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49753179:

The original discussion about the project (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49746163) is very weird. Lots of call-outs about how the author is some sort of celebrity and random accounts vouching for him, with little discussion on the substance.

Not even the demo on that release works well.

Quoting from README:

  • Everything is annotated and nothing is inferred, so code is verbose.
  • No type classes, no traits, and no macros beyond compile-time templates.
  • Bend has no tactics or proof search; proving theorems takes extra effort.
So I think current it's not practical for any serious math formalization.
I agree. What about writing programs and verifying their correctness?

The unofficial guide site https://bend.how/ has many amazing examples across a wide range of areas, mostly about writing programs and partialy verifying their correctness.

There are also math examples, e.g. https://bend.how/math/ proves case 4 for FLT. One thing worth noticing is that it lacks tactics, so the proofs are verbose.

I had thrown some task ideas (e.g. a Lean kernel checker) to Bend 2 and Velvet 2.0 for a comparison, they have very different strengths and current gaps.

This comment from the Haskell subreddit looks informative: https://www.reddit.com/r/haskell/s/elv9QOCOH7.

Quote

A few questions because I am concerned:

  1. Does Bend have decidable type-checking? The Bend VM is not written in Lean, and I don't see a type-checker in Bend.lean. If Bend cannot produce a proof that a typing judgment is right or wrong, there really is no point in advertising it as being able to prevent mistakes via theorem proving techniques.
  2. In BendTT, Type : Type. This is catastrophically dangerous in any type theory but seems to be delivered as a selling point. The justification for this in the BendTT paper is that since no "live" variable can be used more than once, there is no problem. A paper is cited \[16\], but this citation does not say what you think it does. Strong normalization is a trivial result in an affine system, and it does not automatically buy you consistency. These are determined by your inference rules (e.g., a hazardous one like Type : Type). What is the justification for why this does not cause a paradox?
  3. Section 2.2 in the BendTT paper reads, "evaluation is weak head reduction." This is cripplingly restrictive. Bend would not be able to tell that (f x = f y) if (f x) is a stuck term (like a partial application of a function of 2 arguments), even if x = y. The BendTT paper seems to admit this in the last paragraph of Section 2.2: "conversion may diverge on dead code." Why does Bend not use call-by-value semantics? It is the standard.
  4. The BendTT paper is incomprehensible gibberish and is not informative to someone trying to understand your type theory. Several inference rules seem to be missing from the specification. The Lean formalization has 21 constructors for typing judgments. The BendTT paper lists 8. The specification also uses highly unorthodox terminology (e.g., Claude mistakenly referring to De Bruijn indices as a "de Bruijn specification", which is a hallucination and not a term I have ever heard before) and ad-hoc notation, making it difficult to engage with as someone who knows type theory and wants to check your work (or the correctness of the lean formalization, which is also highly obfuscated).

I think it is somewhat irresponsible to be advertising theorem proving software with vibe-coded and flawed foundations. If conversion can diverge in Bend, type-checking cannot be decidable. This is a non-starter for software made to do proofs.

The first point seems wrong. There are legitimate cases of extensional type theories or "ideal" Lean with undecidable typechecking, yes? (Not to be taken as me giving a general defense of Bend or releasing a proof assistant with a Claude-written paper about its type theory.)
I guess you're right. I also get the impression that some type theorists prefer proof assistants that have decidable type checking.

Bulhwi Cha said:

The developers of Bend 2 claim that it outperforms every proof assistant, including Lean, by several OOMs.

Were you able to find the Lean code they were benchmarking against?

I ran some preliminary benchmark method adversarial reviews.

For programs (under runtime/), there are signs where Lean code got some optimizations while Bend code seems to restrain itself from tuning (prompts are given and reflected in comments), but there is no thorough treatment to make the comparison apples-to-apples: Lean is single-threaded and bound-checked, against parallel-by-design Bend code with 16 threads and without bound checks.

For proofs (under checker/, especially proofs_3200 with thousands of inductive types/defs/theorems): Bend is 11-20x vs Rocq, and Lean timed out (300s), likely due to induction/simp elaboration while Bend got explicit proof terms emitted by LLMs upfront. Now I wonder why Rocq is faster and doesn't time out. :joy:

I then ran a Lean vs Rocq on proofs_3200, it turns out that Lean's cost per proof grows with file size, ~12 → 40 → 150 ms, while Rocq's equivalent costs are flat (1.12ms per lemma).

Per-theorem cost of the same corpus (Macbook M4 Pro, but with other current loads):

file theorems user CPU ms/theorem
first 10 units 83 1.01 s 12.2
20 units 163 1.80 s 11.0
100 units 803 11.15 s 13.9
200 units 1,603 26.37 s 16.5
400 units 3,203 128.98 s 40.3
full file 8,537 1,281.85 s 150.2
Rocq, pinned 8,537 9.526 s 1.12
